newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak referendums likely to be declared invalid.
newsitem.headline: Slovak referendums likely to be declared invalid.

text.p: Voting in Slovak referendums, seen as a vital test of the country's commitment to democracy, looked certain to be declared void on Sunday with both government and opposition blaming each other for the failure.

Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar told a news conference less than 10 percent of Slovakia's 3.8 million-strong electorate voted in a referendum thrown into chaos when a question on direct presidential elections was removed at the last minute.

Official results will only be announced when the Central Referendum Committee hands them over to the chairman of parliament but a senior committee official indicated the whole referendum process was likely to be declared void.

"The result is based on the use of invalid ballots and the entire referendum was carried out contrary to the orders of the president of the republic," Jozef Krumpolec, vice-chairman of the Central Referendum Committee told independent Radio Twist.

"The citizens were presented with papers called ballots which we cannot accept," he said. Asked if the committee would officially declare the voting void, Krumpolec said: "I did not say this but you are very close."
Thousands of voters across Slovakia refused to accept the ballot papers, making the three remaining questions on whether Slovakia should join NATO almost irrelevent.
Meciar said that of those who did vote, some 147,000 had voted for NATO membership and 170,000 against.

The proposal on presidential elections was deleted in a feud between President Michal Kovac, who wants future presidents elected directly, and Meciar, who might inherit presidential powers if the choice remains with parliament.
Government and opposition leaders traded blame, and threats of legal action, over the chaos in a process which foreign diplomats had billed as a test of Slovakia's democratic credentials.

"The referendum was important to show who was in favour of NATO and who was trying to prevent this. It was possible to reach a decision which would be favourable to the Slovak Republic but this was foiled," Meciar said.
But he defended Interior Minister Gustav Krajci's decision to remove the question, saying this had been sanctioned by the constitutional court.

"The chaos began when...political parties and the president wrote to the mayors telling them to ignore the government," Meciar said. Kovac had urged voters not to accept ballots without the presidential election question.
Krajci told the news conference Slovaks may be asked to vote again on the question of direct presidential elections if parliament could not reach agreement on the issue.
The opposition said on Sunday it would call an extraordinary session of parliament for June to discuss a new draft law on direct elections.
The referendum appeared to be a blow to Slovakia's stated ambition to be among the first new members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union.
Slovakia's chances of being invited to join NATO after a July alliance summit in Madrid had already waned after U.S. and EU criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
Meciar, accused by his opponents of being lukewarm on NATO membership and of seeking a negative response in the referendum, insisted Slovakia still wanted to join.
"We know we will not be invited to join at Madrid but we shall continue our efforts to join and we know we must improve our image before October when talks start on EU membership," he said.
The dispute over presidential elections springs from a clause in the constitution requiring a three-fifths majority in parliament to elect the president.
If no candidate can muster a sufficient margin, as seems likely on the present strengths of the parties, presidential powers would pass to the prime minister.
